title: When a Massachusetts pharmacist may substitute an interchangeable biological product, and the prescriber's written bar
rule_summary: Under M.G.L. c. 112, § 12EE(b), except as provided in § 12EE(c), a pharmacist filling a prescription for a biological product prescribed by its trade or brand name may substitute an interchangeable biological product. Under § 12EE(c) a pharmacist shall not substitute an interchangeable biological product if the prescriber instructs otherwise in writing, and the instruction shall be on a patient-specific basis. Section 12EE(a) defines an interchangeable biological product as a prescription biological product (i) that has been determined by the United States Food and Drug Administration to be interchangeable with the prescribed brand name biological product pursuant to 42 U.S.C. § 262, or (ii) for which an application has been approved under 21 U.S.C. § 355(b)(2) and which has been determined by the Food and Drug Administration to be therapeutically equivalent to the prescribed brand name biological product, and provides that 'biosimilar' and 'interchangeable' have the same meaning as defined in section 351 of the Public Health Service Act, 42 U.S.C. § 262. It defines a biological product as a virus; therapeutic serum; toxin; antitoxin; vaccine; blood; blood component or derivative; allergenic product; protein, except any chemically synthesized polypeptide, or analogous product; or arsphenamine or derivative of arsphenamine, or any other trivalent organic arsenic compound, applicable to the prevention, treatment or cure of a disease or condition of human beings; and gives practitioner and written prescription the meanings in M.G.L. c. 94C, § 1. Under § 12EE(h) the Department of Public Health may promulgate regulations for implementation and enforcement of the section.
exam_relevance: Tests that biological substitution is a permission rather than a mandate, that it turns on FDA's determination about the particular substitute (interchangeability with the prescribed brand name product, or therapeutic equivalence for a product approved under 21 U.S.C. § 355(b)(2)) rather than on biosimilar status, and that the prescriber's bar is an instruction in writing on a patient-specific basis.

authority.name: Massachusetts General Laws, substitution of interchangeable biological product by pharmacist

exceptions: A pharmacist shall not substitute an interchangeable biological product if the prescriber instructs otherwise in writing; the instruction shall be on a patient-specific basis.
common_confusions: Treating biosimilar status as enough. The statutory definition turns on FDA's determination that the product is interchangeable with the prescribed brand name biological product or, for a product approved under 21 U.S.C. § 355(b)(2), that it is therapeutically equivalent to it.
Reading 'may substitute' as a duty to substitute. M.G.L. c. 112, § 12EE(b) is permissive.
Overlooking the form of the prescriber's bar. M.G.L. c. 112, § 12EE(c) speaks of an instruction in writing, on a patient-specific basis.
verification_notes: Read in the current text of M.G.L. c. 112, § 12EE on malegislature.gov on 2026-09-16, including the definitions in § 12EE(a).
